claim: Each sniff brings in new information, and can be considered as the temporal unit of olfaction.
source: As odorants are carried by air, each sniff brings in new information, and can be considered as the temporal unit of olfaction (Kepecs et al., 2006; Verhagen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kepecs et al., 2006 and Verhagen et al., 2007.

claim: Sniffing can dynamically synchronize with whisking.
source: Sniffing can, however, be more widely seen as patterning sensory processing, as it, for instance, can dynamically synchronize with whisking (Welker, 1964; Cao et al., 2012a; Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Welker, 1964; Cao et al., 2012a; and Moore et al., 2013.

claim: Humans tend to inhale at the start of a cognitive test, even if that does not involve olfaction.
source: A hint that respiration is even more related to brain function comes from the observation that humans tend to inhale at the start of a cognitive test, even if that does not involve olfaction (Perl et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perl et al., 2019.

claim: A change in performance on a visuospatial task varies between inspiration and expiration in line with alteration in the EEG spectrum.
source: This goes so far that a change in performance on a visuospatial task varies between inspiration and expiration was observed in line with alteration in the EEG spectrum (Perl et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perl et al., 2019.

claim: Respiration-induced patterns in neural oscillations are ubiquitously observed throughout the brain.
source: In fact, respiration-induced patterns in neural oscillations are ubiquitously observed throughout the brain (Ito et al., 2014; Yanovsky et al., 2014; Heck et al., 2016; Zelano et al., 2016; Tort et al., 2018; Kluger and Gross, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2014; Yanovsky et al., 2014; Heck et al., 2016; Zelano et al., 2016; Tort et al., 2018; and Kluger and Gross, 2021.

claim: Gamma oscillations (30–100 Hz) can show changes in power that are phase-locked to the respiratory rhythm.
source: Gamma oscillations (30–100 Hz), which could reflect sensorimotor integration (Zagha et al., 2013; Lindeman et al., 2021), can show changes in power that are phase-locked to the respiratory rhythm (Ito et al., 2014; Kluger and Gross, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ito et al., 2014 and Kluger and Gross, 2021.

claim: Respiration can serve as a scaffold for sensory, sensorimotor and cognitive functions.
source: Respiration can, therefore, serve as a scaffold for sensory, sensorimotor and cognitive functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the evidence presented about respiratory coupling with brain rhythms.

claim: Ineffective cardiorespiratory function is an important predictor for development of averse cardiovascular events and mortality.
source: Ineffective cardiorespiratory function is an important predictor for development of averse cardiovascular events and mortality, and has a higher predictive value than for example, smoking or hypertension (Lee et al., 2010; Ross et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2010 and Ross et al., 2016.

claim: The fastigial pressor response entails simultaneous increases in heart rate and arterial pressure with changes in ventilation.
source: An example of the integrated control of cardiovascular and respiratory function is the fastigial pressor response that entails simultaneous increases in heart rate and arterial pressure with changes in ventilation (Miura and Reis, 1969; Achari and Downman, 1970; Lutherer and Williams, 1986; Bradley et al., 1987; Xu and Frazier, 2000; Hernandez et al., 2004; Nisimaru, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miura and Reis, 1969; Achari and Downman, 1970; Lutherer and Williams, 1986; Bradley et al., 1987; Xu and Frazier, 2000; Hernandez et al., 2004; and Nisimaru, 2004.

claim: Lesioning of the fastigial nuclei does lead to impairment of the fastigial pressor response.
source: Yet, lesioning of the fastigial nuclei does lead to impairment of the fastigial pressor response (Zhuang et al., 2008; Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhuang et al., 2008 and illustrated in Figure 8D.

claim: Cardiac and respiratory regulation are coupled on a cycle-by-cycle basis, as the heart rate increases during inspiration, and decreases again during post-inspiration and active expiration.
source: Cardiac and respiratory regulation are coupled on a cycle-by-cycle basis, as the heart rate increases during inspiration, and decreases again during post-inspiration and active expiration (Hirsch and Bishop, 1981; Elstad et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hirsch and Bishop, 1981 and Elstad et al., 2018.

claim: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is caused by respiration-related fluctuations in activity of inhibitory preganglionic parasympathetic cardiac vagal neurons that are primarily located in the nucleus ambiguus.
source: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is caused by respiration-related fluctuations in activity of inhibitory preganglionic parasympathetic cardiac vagal neurons that are primarily located in the nucleus ambiguus (McAllen and Spyer, 1976; Neff et al., 2003; Dergacheva et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McAllen and Spyer, 1976; Neff et al., 2003; and Dergacheva et al., 2010.

claim: The Kölliker-Fuse nucleus provides the phasic excitatory drive to cardiac premotor neurons that is required for respiratory sinus arrhythmia.
source: The Kölliker-Fuse nucleus provides the phasic excitatory drive to these cardiac premotor neurons that is required for respiratory sinus arrhythmia (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Farmer et al., 2016.

claim: Stimulation of pro-opiomelanocortin-producing neurons in the NTS can augment respiratory sinus arrhythmia, along with triggering suppressed breathing (bradypnea) and cardiac function (bradycardia).
source: Stimulation of pro-opiomelanocortin-producing neurons in the NTS can augment respiratory sinus arrhythmia, along with triggering suppressed breathing (bradypnea) and cardiac function (bradycardia) (Cerritelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cerritelli et al., 2016.

claim: The impact of pro-opiomelanocortin on cardiovascular function can be mimicked by administered opioids.
source: Pro-opiomelanocortin is a precursor of the opioid ß-endorphin, and its impact of cardiovascular function can be mimicked by administered opioids (Walker et al., 2007; Izrailtyan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Walker et al., 2007 and Izrailtyan et al., 2018.

claim: The pro-opiomelanocortin neurons of the NTS directly target the pre-Bötzinger complex, giving rise to bradypnea, the ambiguus nucleus, giving rise to bradycardia, and the hypoglossal nucleus, rVRG, and raphe obscurus nucleus.
source: The pro-opiomelanocortin neurons of the NTS directly target important respiratory centers as the pre-Bötzinger complex, giving rise to bradypnea, the ambiguus nucleus, giving rise to bradycardia, and the hypoglossal nucleus, rVRG, hypoglossal nucleus, and raphe obscurus nucleus (Cerritelli et al., 2016; Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cerritelli et al., 2016 and illustrated in Figure 5E.

claim: The pre-Bötzinger complex is essential for inspiration.
source: In particular, the pre-Bötzinger complex is essential in this respect, as inspiration depends on it (Smith et al., 1991; Ramirez et al., 1998; Gray et al., 2001; Tan et al., 2008; Schwarzacher et al., 2011; Ashhad and Feldman, 2020; Dhingra et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Smith et al., 1991; Ramirez et al., 1998; Gray et al., 2001; Tan et al., 2008; Schwarzacher et al., 2011; Ashhad and Feldman, 2020; Dhingra et al., 2020).

claim: Depending on specific behavioral needs, other brain regions may modulate or even overrule the central pattern generators.
source: As all these areas are interconnected (Figure 7), the picture of an integrated network emerges. Thus, depending on specific behavioral needs, these other brain regions may modulate or even overrule the central pattern generators.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the interconnected nature of the respiratory control network.

claim: The respiratory control system should be viewed primarily as an integrated network, rather than a hierarchical system.
source: We therefore suggest to view the respiratory control system primarily as an integrated network, rather than a hierarchical system.
evidence: This is a conclusion and suggestion based on the evidence presented throughout the review.

claim: Integration of behavioral conditions will add to the pathogenesis of respiratory disease.
source: Consequently, we believe that integration of behavioral conditions will add to the pathogenesis of respiratory disease.
evidence: This is a belief statement representing a conclusion drawn from the integrated network perspective.
